S-3_action_links_stores_its_bearer_crede.status: FOUND session 11, NOT FIXED. Needs a migration, so it is blocked by OD-1 behind the same wall as M5.
S-3_action_links_stores_its_bearer_crede.what_the_plan_says: §19 states `S-3` as a residual about `token_prefix`: it 'stores 12 plaintext characters at mint', to be 'declared, bounded, and justified against the remaining entropy, or removed'. That framing assumes the token itself is stored hashed and only a fragment is in the clear.
S-3_action_links_stores_its_bearer_crede.what_is_actually_true: For the `action_links` family the WHOLE TOKEN is in the clear. `20260329165048_remote_schema.sql:947-959` defines `action_links` with a `token text NOT NULL` column and NO `token_hash` column at all. `lib/actionLinks.ts:53` mints `crypto.randomBytes(24).toString('hex')` and `:70` inserts it verbatim. Every consumer selects on the plaintext: `.eq("token", token)` at `action/[token]/route.ts:22`, `action/[token]/consume/route.ts:17`, `action-links/resolve/route.ts:20`, `action-links/consume-accept-job/route.ts:75`, `action-links/consume-reschedule/route.ts:37`.
S-3_action_links_stores_its_bearer_crede.why_it_matters: The entropy is fine — 192 bits — so the credential cannot be guessed. That is not the exposure. The exposure is that the credential is READABLE AT REST: anyone who can read the `action_links` table holds live, replayable, unexpired capabilities for every unconsumed link, and can accept a job, reschedule or cancel as the recipient. That population is larger than it looks, because every service-role path in the product reads with RLS bypassed. A database backup, a log of a query, an over-broad support tool, or any single RLS gap converts directly into action on behalf of recipients. The sibling families already do this correctly — `form_public_links` and the tour links store `token_hash` and never the token — so this is an inconsistency within the codebase, not a standard the product has not yet reached.
S-3_action_links_stores_its_bearer_crede.second_credential_on_the_same_row: `short_code` is an EIGHT-character code over a 55-character alphabet — roughly 46 bits — minted at `lib/actionLinks.ts:69` for SMS-friendly `/a/{code}` URLs and also stored in the clear. It is a second, far weaker credential for the same action. 46 bits is not brute-forceable over the network at any sane rate limit, but it is not 192, and nothing in the tree rate-limits `/a/`. Sized here rather than asserted as a defect.
S-3_action_links_stores_its_bearer_crede.why_it_was_not_fixed_this_session: Converting the family to `token_hash` is a migration plus a change to five routes plus a mint change, and it INVALIDATES EVERY LIVE UNCONSUMED LINK unless it is done as a dual-read window (add `token_hash`, backfill from the plaintext, read either, stop writing plaintext, drop the column). That is a multi-step migration against a shared database whose apply state no worker session can read — OD-1 — and doing the first step without the last leaves the plaintext in place with a second column beside it. It is also a live-credential change for recipients outside the organization, which is a narrowing with a blast radius; W-8 is this initiative's own record of what an unannounced narrowing costs.
S-3_action_links_stores_its_bearer_crede.recommended_disposition: Schedule as its own workstream under W-40 with the dual-read sequence above, after OD-1 gives an apply channel. OD-9.title: W-31 — the product has no server-side password enforcement point. Do we introduce one?
OD-9.status: OPEN — escalated session 11. This is a genuine authentication-architecture decision, which is why it was escalated rather than performed.
OD-9.the_situation: §18 prices W-31 as S–M: 'ship a server-side validator with the current values as defaults', and its exit is 'a policy expressed only in a submit handler no longer exists'. Half of that is now done — the policy has one definition, in `lib/auth/passwordPolicy.ts`, and no caller restates it. The other half cannot be done as priced, because §18 assumes a server-side enforcement point exists to move the check TO, and there is none. The product's only password-setting path is `reset-password:50` — `supabase.auth.updateUser({ password })` — a call from the browser straight to the provider. A grep of the whole tree for a server-side password write (`auth.admin.createUser`, `updateUserById`, any route accepting a `password` field) returns nothing outside test fixtures.
OD-9.the_decision: Does the product introduce a server-mediated password-set route — the browser posts to Alloy, Alloy validates and then calls the provider with the service role — or does it accept that password policy is enforced by the provider's own configuration and by a client-side check, and record that as the position?
OD-9.recommendation: Configure the policy at the provider AND keep the shared module as the client-side expression of it, rather than building a server-mediated route now. A server-mediated password route means Alloy handles plaintext passwords on its own infrastructure, which is a meaningful increase in what a compromise of Alloy costs, in exchange for enforcing a rule Supabase can already enforce at the source. W-33's per-org authentication policy record is where a genuinely per-org rule belongs, and it needs AD-5/AD-7/AD-8 anyway.
OD-9.consequence_of_not_deciding: W-31 stays PARTIAL and the current password floor stays 6 characters, bypassable by anyone who calls `updateUser` directly rather than through the page. That is a small hole — it needs a valid recovery session to reach — but it is open, and the module says so rather than the record quietly claiming the workstream.
OD-9.not_blocking: Nothing else. W-30 and W-32 closed independently.

OD-7.title: W-15 conversion policy — may recording an existing gate as a capability CHANGE who may act?
OD-7.why_it_is_ready_now_and_was_not_before: Session 4 correctly declined to walk 725 handlers in directory order and asked for a policy instead. Session 5 makes that ask answerable: the classes are now measured rather than estimated. 281 handlers enter through a first-party gate helper that is not a capability gate; 144 compare a role or a permission-key array inline; 267 establish the caller and nothing more; 28 carry no discovered authorization, and all but one of those are public by design. The question is not 722 rulings. It is one rule applied to two classes.
OD-7.the_decision: For a handler that today gates on something OTHER than a capability — a role comparison, a portal-eligibility check, a bespoke require* helper — is the conversion required to preserve the current admission set exactly, or may it move to the capability that best expresses the intent even where that widens or narrows who may act?
OD-7.recommendation: Preserve exactly, by default; widen or narrow only per-route with a named decision. Every conversion that changes the admission set is a security change wearing a refactor's clothes, and this initiative already has two isolated instances of precisely that shape (W14-F1's admission half, W49-F1's password-reset control). A preserving conversion is mechanical, reviewable by the existing three joins, and Director-ownable end to end; a changing conversion is not, and should not be smuggled in behind a burndown metric.
alternatives: Preserve exactly (recommended) — the capability chosen must admit precisely today's callers. Consequence: the sweep is mechanical and can proceed without further operator input, but it BANKS existing over-permission rather than fixing it; a route that admits every portal-eligible principal keeps admitting them, now with a capability key naming that fact. The over-permission becomes visible and attributable instead of invisible, which is the point.

Best-expressed intent — pick the capability the route ought to require. Consequence: genuinely fixes over-permission, and cannot be executed without a per-route product judgement about who loses access; every one of those is a potential live lockout, and W-8 already shows what an unannounced narrowing costs.

Split by class — preserve for the 267 authenticated-only handlers, best-intent for the 144 inline role checks. Consequence: defensible, since a raw role comparison is the population most likely to be wrong; but it puts 144 product decisions on the critical path and the lane stalls behind them.
OD-7.consequence_of_not_deciding: The sweep does not start. The declarations are bound and the sizing is trustworthy, so nothing further is gained by more tooling — the next unit of work in this lane is a conversion, and every conversion needs this rule.
OD-7.exact_work_unblocked: The 267 authenticated-only handlers and the 281 gate-helper handlers become a mechanical burndown against the existing three joins under option 1 — the largest single block of remaining W-15 work, and the last structural item standing between the Truthful Access surface and enforcement that matches it.
